ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Thin-lens defocus rendering as supervision for focal-stack depth
PROPOSAL: We train a two-branch network on focal stacks: a focal branch applies 1D convolutions along the stack axis to each pixel's sharpness profile, and a spatial branch applies 2D convolutions on each slice. Their fusion predicts depth and an all-in-focus image, and a differentiable thin-lens renderer re-synthesises the stack from both outputs using the calibrated aperture and focus distances, so that the circle of confusion at each pixel must match the observed blur. Training uses DDFF-12-Scene and FoD500 with ground-truth depth, plus the re-rendering loss on unlabelled smartphone sweeps.
CONTROLS: DDFFNet, DefocusNet and AiFDepthNet retrained on the same splits, a sum-of-modified-Laplacian focus measure with guided filtering, the same network with the renderer removed, and with either branch removed, evaluated by RMSE, absolute relative error and a depth-boundary error on edge pixels.
COST: 320
PREDICTION: The rendering loss should cut boundary error on abrupt depth changes and reduce speckle in low-texture regions compared with every learned baseline; if the renderer branch gives no gain over the fused network alone, the physical model adds nothing beyond the data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Separating texture gradients from depth edges with focus-profile agreement
PROPOSAL: For each pixel we compute the sharpness profile across the stack and its argmax slice, then measure whether neighbouring pixels on each side of a strong image gradient share the same peak slice. A true depth edge separates two peaks, while a texture gradient sits on a single peak. We feed this agreement map, together with the raw stack, to a U-Net that predicts depth, and we add a loss term that penalises depth discontinuities where the agreement map says the peaks coincide. Experiments use DDFF-12-Scene, FoD500 and the Mobile Depth dataset.
CONTROLS: The same U-Net without the agreement map, a version receiving only an all-in-focus image, DefocusNet and DFV as learned references, and a Laplacian focus measure followed by bilateral smoothing, all scored on edge-only pixels and on textured flat regions found from ground truth.
COST: 240
PREDICTION: We expect boundary error to drop on textured flat surfaces, where baselines hallucinate relief, and the ablation without the agreement map should lose most of that gain. The method may fail on reflective surfaces whose peak slice is itself wrong.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learned defocus simulation with a focal-axis regulariser
PROPOSAL: We train a self-supervised model that predicts depth and an all-in-focus image from a focal stack and reconstructs the stack through a learned, spatially varying blur whose kernel size we constrain to be monotone in the distance between the pixel's depth and each slice's focus distance. The monotonicity term regularises the focus behaviour so that sharpness must peak once along the focal axis, and we optimise a second term that smooths depth only across pixels whose sharpness profiles are correlated. We train on unlabelled smartphone sweeps and on 4D Light Field focal stacks, and we evaluate against metric ground truth on DDFF-12-Scene and FoD500.
CONTROLS: The same model with an unconstrained blur kernel, with the correlation-weighted smoothing replaced by an ordinary total-variation prior, AiFDepthNet trained with the same unlabelled data, DDFFNet trained with labels, and a classical sum-of-modified-Laplacian pipeline. Metrics are RMSE, absolute relative error and the fraction of pixels within a threshold ratio of ground truth.
COST: 400
PREDICTION: The monotone kernel should reduce ambiguous focus responses on fine textures and lower RMSE relative to the unconstrained model, with the largest gains on sparsely sampled stacks. If the unconstrained kernel does equally well, the physical constraint is already learned implicitly from the data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Sparse stacks and noisy slices as a stress test for physics-aware focus models
PROPOSAL: We ask whether a model that reads the stack along its focal axis stays accurate when the stack becomes sparse. We build a network whose first stage fits, per pixel, a parametric sharpness curve across slices using the thin-lens relation between depth and circle of confusion (CoC) diameter, and whose second stage refines the curve parameters spatially with an edge-aware convolutional neural network (CNN). We train on the Focus-on-Defocus benchmark (FoD500) and on focal stacks rendered from the New York University Depth version two dataset (NYU Depth v2), then evaluate with stacks subsampled to a quarter of their slices and with added sensor noise.
CONTROLS: DefocusNet and a deep focus volume network retrained under the same subsampling, a Laplacian focus measure with guided filtering, our model with the parametric stage replaced by a free per-pixel argmax, and the full stack as an upper reference, reported as root mean square error (RMSE) and absolute relative error on all pixels and on depth-edge pixels.
COST: 280
PREDICTION: The parametric curve should degrade gracefully as slices are removed, while the argmax variant and the learned baselines should lose accuracy sharply below eight slices. Gains may vanish on reflective regions where no single sharpness peak exists.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reflective and low-texture regions handled by focus-confidence gating
PROPOSAL: We estimate, for every pixel, a confidence in its focus cue from the peakedness of the sharpness profile along the stack, and we train a depth network whose spatial propagation is gated by this confidence: pixels with a flat or multi-modal profile receive depth propagated from confident neighbours along image structure rather than from their own focus response. The confidence head is supervised by whether the argmax slice matches ground-truth depth within a tolerance. Training uses DDFF-12-Scene and FoD500, with evaluation on a held-out set of scenes containing glass, metal and plain walls that we annotate by region type.
CONTROLS: The same network with uniform gating, a variant with confidence from a sum-of-modified-Laplacian response alone, DDFFNet and AiFDepthNet retrained on the same splits, and a classical pipeline with post-hoc smoothing. We report RMSE per region type and a depth-boundary error.
COST: 260
PREDICTION: Gated propagation should lower RMSE on reflective and low-texture regions without blurring edges elsewhere, and the uniform-gating variant should match it only on well-textured regions. If confidence from the simple Laplacian response works as well as the learned head, the learned head is not needed.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Focal-axis attention versus 3D convolution for focal-stack depth
PROPOSAL: We compare two ways of reading the focal dimension: a transformer that attends across slices at each spatial location before a spatial decoder, and a 3D convolutional encoder that mixes spatial and focal axes jointly. Both receive the same per-slice features and the slice focus distances as positional codes. We train both on DDFF-12-Scene and on synthetic stacks rendered from NYU Depth v2 with a thin-lens blur, and test on FoD500 and on real smartphone sweeps with stacks of varying length.
CONTROLS: DefocusNet and DFV as published designs retrained on our splits, a per-slice 2D encoder with max pooling over slices, the focal transformer with shuffled slice order to test whether it uses the focal structure, and a classical Laplacian focus measure with guided filter smoothing, with three seeds per configuration.
COST: 360
PREDICTION: The focal transformer should generalise better to stacks of lengths unseen in training than the 3D convolutional encoder, and both should beat the pooled 2D encoder on abrupt depth changes. If shuffling the slice order costs nothing, the model reads appearance rather than focus evolution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cross-dataset transfer of focal-stack depth under camera changes
PROPOSAL: We test whether a depth-from-focus model that takes the calibrated focus distances and aperture as input transfers across cameras. We train a network that normalises each slice's focus distance by the camera's hyperfocal distance and predicts depth in units of the circle-of-confusion scale, then converts to metric depth with the calibration. Training uses DDFF-12-Scene, and we evaluate zero-shot on FoD500 and on the Mobile Depth dataset, which come from different lenses, before and after fine-tuning on a small subset of each.
CONTROLS: The same network without calibration inputs, DDFFNet and AiFDepthNet trained identically, a monocular relative-depth model aligned to ground truth by least squares as a scale-free comparison, and a classical focus measure with per-camera depth lookup. We report RMSE, absolute relative error and the ratio of errors before and after fine-tuning.
COST: 300
PREDICTION: Calibration-aware prediction should transfer with far less loss than the uncalibrated network, whose errors should scale with the mismatch in aperture between cameras. We may see no benefit on the Mobile Depth dataset if its calibration metadata is too coarse.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Synthetic focal stacks with controlled texture to isolate texture-induced depth errors
PROPOSAL: We render focal stacks from NYU Depth v2 and from procedurally generated scenes where we control, per surface, the texture frequency, the presence of repeating patterns and the sharpness of depth discontinuities, using a thin-lens blur with a calibrated circle of confusion. We train a depth network on this data with a loss that weights depth-gradient errors by the mismatch between image gradients and ground-truth depth gradients, so that the model learns to discount gradients that do not correspond to depth. We then evaluate on real DDFF-12-Scene and FoD500 stacks.
CONTROLS: Training on the same renders with an unweighted L1 loss, DefocusNet and DFV trained on the same renders, a classical sum-of-modified-Laplacian pipeline, and an evaluation split of real scenes with high-frequency textures on flat surfaces, scored by RMSE and by the number of spurious depth edges found by a Canny detector on the depth map.
COST: 220
PREDICTION: The gradient-mismatch weighting should reduce spurious depth edges on textured flat surfaces by a wide factor while leaving RMSE on true edges unchanged. The gain may not transfer to real stacks if the synthetic blur differs from real lens behaviour.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Joint depth and all-in-focus estimation with sharpness consistency
PROPOSAL: We train a network that outputs depth and an all-in-focus image together and enforce consistency between them: the all-in-focus image, blurred at each pixel according to the predicted depth and each slice's focus distance, must reproduce the input stack, and the sharpness of the all-in-focus image must exceed that of every slice at every pixel. The second constraint penalises depth estimates that pick a slice where the scene point is still blurred, which happens in low-texture regions. Training uses DDFF-12-Scene with labels and unlabelled 4D Light Field stacks, with evaluation on FoD500.
CONTROLS: AiFDepthNet, which also reconstructs the stack but without the sharpness constraint, DefocusNet trained with labels only, the same network trained without the sharpness term, and a classical focus measure with guided filter smoothing. We report RMSE, absolute relative error, and a boundary error on depth edges.
COST: 340
PREDICTION: The sharpness constraint should reduce errors in low-texture regions where the reconstruction loss alone is nearly flat in depth. If the term brings no gain over AiFDepthNet retrained on our data, the reconstruction loss already captures it.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Noise-aware focus volumes for sharp, clean depth maps
PROPOSAL: We build a focus volume whose per-slice sharpness is computed by a learned operator trained to be invariant to sensor noise, using pairs of clean and noise-augmented stacks, and we decode depth from this volume with a cost-volume style soft argmax followed by a learned edge-preserving filter that takes the all-in-focus image as guidance. Training uses DDFF-12-Scene and FoD500 with photometric noise augmentation, and we evaluate on real stacks captured in low light with the Mobile Depth dataset and our own additions.
CONTROLS: DFV with its fixed Laplacian focus volume, DDFFNet, a classical focus measure with and without denoising applied to the slices beforehand, and our model with the learned operator swapped for a Laplacian, evaluated at several noise levels by RMSE and by a measure of speckle in flat regions.
COST: 200
PREDICTION: The learned operator should keep RMSE nearly flat as noise rises, while the Laplacian-based volumes degrade quickly. If denoising the slices first closes the gap, a learned operator is not needed.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Spatial and focal branches fused for indoor depth from focus
PROPOSAL: Train a two-branch network on the DDFF 12-Scene and FoD500 focal stacks. A spatial branch encodes structure across neighbouring pixels with learned gradient filters, and a focal branch encodes each pixel's sharpness profile across slices with a one-dimensional convolution. A fusion head outputs a depth map and a confidence map. Optimise with AdamW, a batch of 8, an L1 depth loss and an edge-aware smoothness term. Report RMSE, absolute relative error, the fraction of pixels within a factor 1.25 of the reference depth, and an edge F-score around depth discontinuities.
CONTROLS: Compare against the published DFV network and a Laplacian-variance focus measure on identical focal stacks with the same crop. Compare against a variant that feeds the stack as generic channels with the same parameter count. Compare edge accuracy on textured patches against depth-discontinuity patches under the same evaluation mask. Repeat training with five seeds and report the spread of every metric.
COST: 120
PREDICTION: Expect lower RMSE and sharper edges than the published DFV network, with the largest gains in low-texture regions. The claim fails if the gain vanishes on reflective surfaces or if the edge F-score does not improve over the generic-channel variant.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Structure and focus streams combined to refine indoor depth maps
PROPOSAL: Build a dual-stream model trained on DDFF 12-Scene and FoD500 stacks. A structure stream applies learned derivative filters over adjacent pixels while a focus stream runs a one-dimensional convolution along the slice axis for every pixel; a fusion head predicts depth together with an uncertainty map. Training relies on AdamW, a batch of 8, an L1 loss on depth and an edge-aware smoothness penalty. Evaluation covers RMSE, absolute relative error, the share of pixels within a factor 1.25 of the reference depth, and an edge F-score near depth discontinuities.
CONTROLS: Compare against a published monocular depth network and a Sobel edge detector on identical all-in-focus images with the same crop. Compare against a variant with a wider backbone with the same slice count. Compare edge accuracy on bright patches against dark patches under the same evaluation mask. Repeat training with five seeds and report the spread of every metric.
COST: 120
PREDICTION: Expect lower RMSE and sharper edges than the published monocular network, with the largest gains in low-texture regions. The claim fails if the gain vanishes on reflective surfaces or if the edge F-score does not improve over the wider variant.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Thin-lens sharpness curves for depth from sparse focal stacks
PROPOSAL: Predict, for every pixel, the parameters of a thin-lens sharpness curve over focus distance and read depth from the curve peak. A ResNet-34 encoder with a feature pyramid takes each slice, a transformer layer mixes information along the slice axis, and a head regresses curve centre and width. Train on DDFF 12-Scene with an L1 depth loss and a curve-fit loss, using AdamW and a batch of 8. Evaluate RMSE and absolute relative error on the held-out scenes when the stack is subsampled to 3, 5 and 10 slices.
CONTROLS: Compare the curve-peak depth with the argmax-over-slices depth from the same network features. Vary the number of input slices while the training schedule is held fixed. Add Gaussian noise at matched levels to every stack and compare errors with the reference run. Repeat evaluation on a held-out scene split with five seeds.
COST: 300
PREDICTION: Expect the curve-peak readout to degrade more slowly than the argmax readout as slices are removed. It is refuted if the gap closes under noise or if the error with 3 slices is not below the argmax error.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Curve-based depth readout with a lightweight convolutional encoder
PROPOSAL: Regress per-pixel sharpness curves over focus distance and take depth at the curve maximum. A ResNet-34 trunk with a feature pyramid processes every slice, one attention layer exchanges information across slices, and a prediction head returns curve centre and width. Training uses DDFF 12-Scene, an L1 depth loss plus a curve-fit loss, AdamW and a batch of 8. Report RMSE and absolute relative error on held-out scenes for stacks subsampled to 3, 5 and 10 slices.
CONTROLS: Compare the curve-peak depth with the depth from the same network features after a colour-space change. Vary the augmentation strength while the training schedule is held fixed. Add shifted crops at matched positions to every stack and compare errors with the reference run. Repeat evaluation on a held-out scene split with five seeds.
COST: 300
PREDICTION: Expect the curve-peak readout to degrade more slowly than a plain maximum readout as slices are removed. It is refuted if the gap closes under augmentation or if the error with 3 slices is not below the colour-space error.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Metric depth from a relative-depth prior and a focal stack
PROPOSAL: Start from a frozen Depth Anything V2 model that outputs relative depth for the middle slice, and fuse it with a lightweight focal encoder that supplies metric scale through sharpness peaks. A cross-attention module lets prior features query focal features, and a scale head regresses a per-pixel scale and shift. Fine-tune on DDFF 12-Scene indoor stacks with an L1 loss and a gradient-matching loss, AdamW, and a batch of 4. Report RMSE and absolute relative error, split by region type.
CONTROLS: Evaluate on low-texture and reflective regions defined by a local variance mask. Compare against the relative-depth prior with a global scale-and-shift fitted to the reference depth. Subsample the stack to five slices and compare with the full stack under the same schedule. Repeat on stacks from a second camera with five seeds.
COST: 80
PREDICTION: Expect the largest gain over the prior in reflective and low-texture regions, where relative depth is least reliable. The claim fails if the fused model matches the scale-and-shift fit there, or if the error rises sharply on the second camera.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Focal-stack refinement of a pretrained relative-depth network
PROPOSAL: Attach a small focal encoder to a frozen Depth Anything V2 network, which reads the central slice only. The encoder turns sharpness peaks into metric scale, and a cross-attention module lets the network's features query it before a scale head returns per-pixel scale and shift. Fine-tuning uses indoor DDFF 12-Scene stacks, an L1 loss with a gradient-matching term, AdamW and a batch of 4. RMSE and absolute relative error are broken down by region type.
CONTROLS: Evaluate on high-texture and matte regions defined by a local variance mask. Compare against the relative-depth prior with a global scale-and-shift fitted to the reference depth. Subsample the stack to nine slices and compare with the full stack under the same schedule. Repeat on stacks from the same camera with five seeds.
COST: 80
PREDICTION: Expect a clear gain over the prior in matte and high-texture regions, where fused depth should look cleaner. The claim fails if the fused model matches the scale-and-shift fit there, or if the error rises sharply on the nine-slice stacks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cross-slice gradient consistency to separate texture from depth edges
PROPOSAL: Add a consistency module to a depth-from-focus network. A depth discontinuity shifts the gradient direction between slices as blur grows, whereas a surface pattern keeps its position. The module compares gradient maps from adjacent slices, produces an edge-likelihood map, and gates the smoothness term with it. Train on DDFF 12-Scene and FoD500 with an L1 loss, AdamW and a batch of 8. Report RMSE, absolute relative error, and edge precision and recall.
CONTROLS: Measure edge precision and recall of the predicted depth map against depth discontinuities in the ground truth, using the same tolerance in pixels. Compare on a texture-swapped test set in which printed patterns are applied to flat surfaces. Report the false-edge rate at textured but flat locations for the gated and ungated models. Repeat training with five seeds.
COST: 200
PREDICTION: Expect fewer false edges on textured flat surfaces and higher edge precision at similar recall. The result is refuted if the false-edge rate is unchanged after gating, or if recall drops by more than a few points.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gradient-aware smoothness gating for focal-stack depth networks
PROPOSAL: Extend a depth-from-focus network with a gating module. Gradient maps taken from neighbouring slices are compared, an edge-likelihood map is predicted from their differences, and this map modulates the smoothness term during training. The backbone is a 3D encoder-decoder trained on DDFF 12-Scene and FoD500 with an L1 loss, AdamW and a batch of 8. Evaluation reports RMSE, absolute relative error, and the precision and recall of predicted edges.
CONTROLS: Measure gradient magnitude of the predicted depth map against gradient magnitude of the all-in-focus image, using the same tolerance in pixels. Compare on a brightness-shifted test set in which exposure changes are applied to flat surfaces. Report the mean absolute error over all pixels for the gated and ungated models. Repeat training with five seeds.
COST: 200
PREDICTION: Expect closer agreement in gradient magnitude and lower pixel error under gating. The result is refuted if the error is unchanged after gating, or if the agreement drops by more than a few points.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Joint spatial-focal attention for robust focal-stack depth
PROPOSAL: Replace generic 3D convolutions with factorised attention: spatial attention within each slice, then focal attention along the slice axis at every pixel, used in four blocks with a shared positional encoding for slice index. Train on DDFF 12-Scene with a combined L1 and scale-invariant loss, AdamW and a batch of 8. Report RMSE, absolute relative error and edge F-score, and show qualitative maps for fine-textured scenes and abrupt depth changes.
CONTROLS: Compare the joint model against a spatial-only variant and a focal-only variant, each with matched parameters. Evaluate each variant on fine-textured and abrupt-depth-change regions using the same masks. Vary the number of slices for every variant while the learning rate is held fixed. Repeat training with five seeds.
COST: 450
PREDICTION: Expect the joint model to lead on fine textures and abrupt changes, with a smaller gain elsewhere. The claim fails if either single-branch variant matches the joint model on those regions, or if the ranking flips across seeds.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Factorised attention blocks over image and focus axes
PROPOSAL: Swap generic 3D convolutions for two-stage attention: one stage attends across pixels of a single slice, the next attends along the slice axis for each pixel, stacked in four blocks that share a slice-index positional encoding. Training uses DDFF 12-Scene, a combined L1 and scale-invariant loss, AdamW and a batch of 8. Metrics are RMSE, absolute relative error and edge F-score, with qualitative maps for fine-textured scenes and abrupt depth changes.
CONTROLS: Compare the joint model against a spatial-only variant doubled in depth and a variant with the block order swapped, each with matched parameters. Evaluate each variant on image-centre and image-border regions using the same masks. Vary the weight decay for every variant while the learning rate is held fixed. Repeat training with five seeds.
COST: 450
PREDICTION: Expect the joint model to lead on image-centre regions and to keep that lead on image-border regions. The claim fails if the depth-doubled variant matches the joint model there, or if the ranking flips across seeds.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Parametric sharpness curves fitted along the focal axis
PROPOSAL: We model each pixel's sharpness as a function of slice focus distance given by the thin-lens circle-of-confusion relation, with depth and a texture amplitude as parameters, and train a network to regress these parameters from the raw stack, followed by a spatial module that shares parameters among pixels with similar profiles. Because the curve shape is fixed by optics, ambiguous or noisy responses are read as poor fits rather than as depth. We train on DDFF-12-Scene and FoD500 and test on sparse and noisy stacks.
CONTROLS: DefocusNet, DFV and AiFDepthNet retrained identically, a classical Laplacian focus measure with guided filtering, the same network with a free per-pixel argmax instead of the parametric fit, and a version without the spatial module, scored by RMSE, boundary error and fit residual, on full, half and quarter stacks, with bootstrap intervals over scenes and inference time per stack.
COST: 560
PREDICTION: The parametric model should degrade least on sparse stacks and should flag reflective regions by high residual. If the free argmax matches it on quarter stacks, the optical curve carries no extra information.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Fine-tuning a monocular depth foundation model on the sharpest focal slice
PROPOSAL: We select, for each focal stack, the slice with the highest global sharpness, fine-tune a large pretrained relative-depth transformer on these single images with metric ground truth from DDFF-12-Scene and FoD500, and recover metric scale through a small head that reads the camera focus distance of the chosen slice. The approach uses the mature single-image pipeline and avoids processing the whole stack, which should make it light and simple to deploy on phones.
CONTROLS: Baselines are the pretrained transformer with least-squares scale alignment, DefocusNet and DDFFNet on the same splits, and a classical sum-of-modified-Laplacian pipeline. Ablations vary the slice-selection rule, the size of the fine-tuned backbone, and freezing versus training the encoder, scored by RMSE and absolute relative error over three seeds.
COST: 560
PREDICTION: The fine-tuned model should approach the learned focal-stack baselines on RMSE and beat the classical pipeline. If it loses badly on scenes with abrupt depth changes, single-image priors do not substitute for the focal cue, and the claim fails.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Focal-order permutation to test whether networks read focus evolution
PROPOSAL: We train a focal-stack network with an explicit module that encodes the ordering of slices and their focus distances and that computes finite differences of features along the focal axis, and we test whether this module forces the model to use focus evolution rather than appearance. Training uses DDFF-12-Scene and FoD500, with evaluation on both and on smartphone sweeps.
CONTROLS: DDFFNet, DefocusNet and DFV are each trained on correctly ordered stacks and on stacks whose slice order is permuted at training time, against our model under the same two conditions, plus a classical focus measure, scored by RMSE, boundary error and errors on textured flat regions, with the published numbers of each baseline listed as a sanity check on our retraining.
COST: 180
PREDICTION: Baselines should lose little under permutation, revealing that they read appearance, while our model should lose much and should outperform them on textured flat regions in the ordered setting. If our model also survives permutation, the finite-difference module is bypassed.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: All-in-focus image synthesis from focal stacks with a diffusion prior
PROPOSAL: We train a conditional diffusion model that takes a focal stack and synthesises an all-in-focus image, using a pretrained image diffusion backbone adapted with a stack encoder, and we assess whether the synthesised image preserves fine textures and sharp object boundaries better than fusion rules that pick the sharpest slice per pixel. Training uses DDFF-12-Scene and the 4D Light Field dataset, where all-in-focus references exist, with evaluation on FoD500.
CONTROLS: We compare against the per-pixel sharpest-slice composite, a guided-filter fusion, and the all-in-focus output of AiFDepthNet, measuring PSNR, SSIM and a learned perceptual metric, and we ablate the stack encoder depth and the number of sampling steps, with a slice-shuffled conditioning as placebo and inference time reported.
COST: 180
PREDICTION: The diffusion model should produce the best perceptual scores and fewer fusion seams at boundaries. If PSNR drops while the perceptual score rises, the model hallucinates texture.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Self-supervised focal-stack depth with a monotone learned blur
PROPOSAL: We learn depth and an all-in-focus image from unlabelled focal stacks by reconstructing each slice through a spatially varying blur whose size is constrained to grow monotonically with the distance between the pixel depth and the slice focus distance, as thin-lens optics requires. A gradient term smooths depth only across pixels whose sharpness profiles correlate, so texture gradients do not create depth steps. We train on unlabelled smartphone sweeps and 4D Light Field stacks and evaluate on DDFF-12-Scene and FoD500 against metric ground truth.
CONTROLS: AiFDepthNet trained on the same unlabelled data, the model with an unconstrained blur, the model with plain total-variation smoothing, DDFFNet trained with labels as a supervised reference, and a classical Laplacian pipeline, scored by RMSE, boundary error and false-edge counts, with loss curves kept to check that the monotone constraint does not slow convergence.
COST: 720
PREDICTION: The monotone blur should give lower RMSE than the unconstrained one and fewer false edges than total variation. If the supervised reference is far ahead on all metrics, self-supervision with optics is not yet competitive and the claim is refuted.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learned slice selection to compress focal stacks before depth estimation
PROPOSAL: We train a selector network that scores each slice of a focal stack and keeps the four most informative ones, aiming to reduce capture and storage on phones, then run an unchanged pretrained DefocusNet on the reduced stack. The selector is trained by reinforcement with the downstream RMSE as reward, on DDFF-12-Scene and FoD500, with evaluation on both plus smartphone sweeps of varying length, where the selector sees stacks longer than those it was trained on.
CONTROLS: Comparisons are uniform subsampling, random subsampling, selecting the slices with the highest mean Laplacian response, and the full stack as an upper reference, with DefocusNet and DFV as downstream networks. We ablate the number of kept slices from two to eight and report RMSE, absolute relative error and the selector's inference time over three seeds.
COST: 720
PREDICTION: Learned selection should recover most of the full-stack accuracy with four slices and beat uniform subsampling clearly. If the Laplacian heuristic matches it, the learned selector has to be dropped.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Rendered focal stacks with controlled texture and depth discontinuities
PROPOSAL: We render focal stacks from NYU Depth v2 and procedural scenes with a thin-lens blur, controlling per surface the texture frequency, repeating patterns and the sharpness of depth steps, and train a network with a loss that down-weights depth-gradient errors where the image gradient is not matched by a true depth gradient. The data lets us measure separately errors caused by texture and errors caused by depth steps, and the loss should teach the model to discount texture gradients. We evaluate on real DDFF-12-Scene and FoD500 stacks.
CONTROLS: The same network with a plain L1 loss on the same renders, DefocusNet and DFV trained on the renders, training on real data only, a classical sum-of-modified-Laplacian pipeline, and metrics of RMSE, boundary error and false depth edges on textured flat surfaces, stratified by texture frequency, with bootstrap intervals over test scenes.
COST: 420
PREDICTION: False depth edges should drop sharply on high-frequency textures, and the stratified curves should show where the model still fails. If the gain disappears on real stacks, the synthetic blur does not match real lenses.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Benchmarking focus-measure operators and smoothing for focal-stack depth
PROPOSAL: We systematically evaluate classical focus-measure operators, including sum-of-modified-Laplacian, Tenengrad, variance of Laplacian, wavelet energy and a frequency-domain contrast measure, each combined with Gaussian, bilateral or guided-filter smoothing at several window sizes, to establish which combination gives the best metric depth on DDFF-12-Scene, FoD500 and smartphone sweeps, and we tune each pipeline on a validation split before testing. The outcome is a tuned classical pipeline and a table of failure cases by scene type for future work.
CONTROLS: Each operator is tested with and without noise added to the slices, with full and subsampled stacks, and against DefocusNet and DDFFNet as learned references, scored by RMSE, absolute relative error and boundary error with bootstrap intervals over scenes, and the inference time of each pipeline on a laptop processor.
COST: 420
PREDICTION: Wavelet energy with guided filtering should win among classical methods but stay behind the learned references. If any operator approaches the learned models on boundary error, the learned gains come mostly from smoothing rather than from the networks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Slice-wise attention with focus-distance encoding for focal stacks
PROPOSAL: We build a model whose per-pixel encoder attends across slices using the slice focus distances as continuous positional codes, then passes the attended features to a spatial decoder with edge-aware upsampling. The attention lets the model compare sharpness between any two slices directly, which should help when the focus response is ambiguous, and the positional codes let it handle stacks of any length and spacing. Training uses DDFF-12-Scene and FoD500, and we test on stacks of lengths and spacings unseen in training.
CONTROLS: DefocusNet, DFV and DDFFNet retrained with the same data, a 3D convolutional encoder of equal size and inference time, the attention model without focus-distance codes, a classical Laplacian pipeline, and tests on stacks subsampled or re-spaced at inference, with RMSE, boundary error and errors on textured flat regions, over three seeds.
COST: 300
PREDICTION: The attention model should keep its accuracy on unseen stack lengths where the 3D encoder breaks down, and should beat it on abrupt depth changes. If removing the codes changes nothing, the model ignores focus geometry.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Estimating lens parameters from focal stacks with a regression network
PROPOSAL: We train a network to regress the aperture, focal length and per-slice focus distance of a focal stack from the images alone, using DDFF-12-Scene and FoD500 where these values are known, with rendered stacks from NYU Depth v2 as additional data. Accurate self-calibration would let classical depth-from-focus pipelines run on stacks whose metadata is missing or coarse, as on many phones, and would also tell how far the thin-lens model holds for real lenses.
CONTROLS: Baselines are the metadata values themselves, a least-squares fit of the thin-lens model to Laplacian peak positions, and a model trained on rendered data only. We ablate the backbone size and the number of slices given to the regressor, and report relative error per parameter and the RMSE of a classical pipeline run with the predicted versus true parameters, over three seeds.
COST: 300
PREDICTION: The network should recover focus distances within a small relative error and aperture less well. If the downstream depth RMSE barely changes between predicted and true parameters, calibration is not the limiting factor.
